name: South Africa
governanceModel: Decentralized, sector-based oversight built on existing regulators (data protection, financial, health) rather than a standalone AI law, with a national AI policy currently being redrafted after a citation scandal

Whether a decentralized, sector-regulator model can substitute for a dedicated AI law
overview:
South Africa does not have a standalone AI act, and its approach to date has combined a sector-by-sector regulatory model with a slow-moving national AI policy process. The Department of Communications and Digital Technologies (DCDT) released an initial AI Policy Framework in October 2024, proposing to lean on existing bodies — the Information Regulator under the Protection of Personal Information Act (POPIA), the Financial Sector Conduct Authority and South African Reserve Bank for financial AI, and the South African Health Products Regulatory Authority (SAHPRA) for medical AI — rather than create a single AI super-regulator, alongside a four-tier risk classification broadly modelled on the EU AI Act.

That process suffered a significant setback in April 2026: after Cabinet published a draft National AI Policy for public comment on April 2, 2026, reporting on April 26 revealed that at least several of the document's roughly 67 references were AI-fabricated, non-existent citations. Minister of Communications and Digital Technologies Solly Malatsi withdrew the draft on April 27, 2026, calling the episode "embarrassing" and pledging consequences for those responsible for drafting and quality assurance. In May 2026, Malatsi appointed an independent expert panel — chaired by Wits University's Professor Benjamin Rosman and including Professor Vukosi Marivate, Professor Alison Gillwald of Research ICT Africa, and others — to authenticate references and guide a redraft, with the revised policy targeted for Cabinet submission by November 2026 and public comment expected around January 2027.

currentDirection.summary: South Africa's AI governance trajectory was disrupted rather than accelerated in 2026: the government's first attempt at a full National AI Policy was withdrawn after a citation-fabrication scandal, and the policy is now being rebuilt by an independent academic-led panel with a target of reaching Cabinet by around November 2026. In the interim, existing sector regulators (data protection, financial, health) continue to apply general law to AI use cases, and no dedicated AI statute has been introduced in Parliament.

During its 2025 G20 presidency, South Africa foregrounds AI and digital public infrastructure as headline themes — convening a G20 Task Force on AI, Data Governance and Innovation for Sustainable Development and promoting an 'AI for Africa' agenda — before the rotating presidency passes to the United States for 2026.

policyAndRegulation.title: Protection of Personal Information Act (POPIA)
policyAndRegulation.summary: General data-protection law enforced by the Information Regulator; forms the main current legal lever over AI systems that process personal data, including automated decision-making.

policyAndRegulation.title: National AI Policy Framework
policyAndRegulation.summary: October 2024 discussion document from the DCDT proposing sector-based, risk-tiered AI oversight; a preliminary framework rather than binding law, superseded in status by the since-withdrawn 2026 draft policy.

policyAndRegulation.title: Draft National AI Policy (2026)
policyAndRegulation.summary: Published for public comment on April 2, 2026, then withdrawn on April 27, 2026, after being found to contain AI-fabricated citations. Being rebuilt by an independent expert panel, with Cabinet submission targeted for around November 2026.

researchEcosystem.summary: South African AI research is anchored significantly at the University of the Witwatersrand (Wits), whose School of Computer Science and Applied Mathematics and Machine Intelligence and Neural Discovery (MIND) Institute host a notable concentration of AI researchers on the continent, and which hosted the first Deep Learning Indaba in 2017 — a pan-African machine learning conference founded partly in response to the near-total absence of African-institution papers at top ML venues. Research ICT Africa, based in Cape Town and affiliated with the University of Cape Town, is a leading policy-research think tank on AI and digital rights across Africa, led by founding director Professor Alison Gillwald.

notableGaps.note: South Africa's draft National AI Policy was withdrawn in April 2026 after fabricated citations were discovered; as of mid-2026 there is no adopted national AI policy, only the 2024 preliminary framework and a redraft in progress.

South Africa has explicitly chosen not to create a standalone AI regulator, relying instead on existing sector bodies (Information Regulator, FSCA, SAHPRA) — a deliberate design choice rather than an oversight gap, but one whose coordination mechanisms remain unbuilt while the national policy is being redrafted.

debates.topic: Withdrawal of the draft National AI Policy over AI-fabricated citations and what it means for government AI use
debates.summary: The April 2026 withdrawal of South Africa's draft National AI Policy, after its reference list was found to contain AI-generated fictitious sources, became a widely discussed cautionary case about unverified AI use inside government itself.
debates.expanded: Minister Malatsi described the episode as a failure of human oversight rather than of the policy's substantive content, and pledged consequences for those responsible for drafting and quality assurance. Commentators, including some South African legal and media outlets, characterised the incident as "embarrassing and damning," and it has fed into the broader debate about how the government can credibly regulate AI risk (including hallucination and verification failures) while its own drafting processes remain vulnerable to the same failure modes.

debates.topic: Whether a decentralized, sector-regulator model can substitute for a dedicated AI law
debates.summary: South Africa's policy approach — leaning on the Information Regulator, FSCA, SAHPRA and other existing bodies rather than a single AI authority — is a deliberate design choice that remains contested among policy observers.
debates.expanded: Proponents argue this avoids duplicating regulatory expertise and lets AI oversight be embedded in bodies that already understand their sectors. Critics, including some of the independent panel members now redrafting the policy, have raised concerns about coordination gaps, unclear escalation paths for cross-sectoral AI harms, and the fact that the coordinating bodies proposed in the withdrawn draft (a National AI Coordination Office, inter-departmental forums, an AI Advisory Council) would lack binding enforcement powers even once established.
